sentence: The NHS describes citalopram as an antidepressant that is often used to treat low mood and depression.
note: NHS: often used to treat low mood (depression).

sentence: It is also sometimes used for panic attacks.
note: NHS: also sometimes used for panic attacks.

sentence: It belongs to a group of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs.
note: NHS: an antidepressant called an SSRI.

sentence: Stopping an antidepressant too early can let depression come back.
note: NHS antidepressants page: stopping before the recommended time can make depression return.

sentence: For citalopram, the NHS says people usually need to take it for at least 6 months.
note: NHS common questions: usually need to take it for at least 6 months.

sentence: SSRIs such as citalopram are thought to work by raising the level of serotonin in the brain.
note: NHS: thought to work by increasing serotonin levels in the brain.

sentence: Serotonin is thought to have a good effect on mood, emotion and sleep.
note: NHS: serotonin thought to have a good effect on mood, emotion and sleep.

sentence: The NHS says citalopram may start to work on symptoms after one or two weeks.
note: NHS: may take 1 or 2 weeks before it starts to work.

sentence: It usually takes between four and six weeks before the full benefit is felt.
note: NHS: usually 4 to 6 weeks for full benefits.

sentence: The NHS advises giving it at least six weeks, and talking to the doctor if there is no improvement by then.
note: NHS: give at least 6 weeks; if no better after 6 weeks talk to doctor.

sentence: Some people feel worse in the first few weeks before they begin to feel better.
note: NHS: some people feel worse during first few weeks before improving.

sentence: The NHS lists headaches, feeling sick, being sick and sweating among the common side effects.
note: NHS: common side effects include headaches, nausea, vomiting, sweating.

sentence: Most side effects ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.
note: NHS: most side effects should ease after a couple of weeks.

sentence: More serious side effects are rare.
note: NHS: more serious side effects are rare.

sentence: Serotonin syndrome is a rare but serious condition that causes a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles, and feeling confused or agitated.
note: NHS side effects: serotonin syndrome described with these features.

sentence: A rare, life-threatening heart rhythm problem can cause a fast, irregular heartbeat, light-headedness and fainting.
note: NHS: torsades de pointes causes fast irregular heartbeat, light-headedness, fainting.

sentence: Low sodium in the blood can show as headaches, trouble concentrating, memory problems, weakness, seizures or loss of balance.
note: NHS: signs of low sodium listed.

sentence: The NHS says to call NHS 111 if someone taking citalopram thinks they may be having serious side effects.
note: NHS: call 111 if you think you have serious side effects.

sentence: Chest pain, a first seizure, fainting, or thoughts of harming oneself or ending one's life need a call to 999 or a trip to A&E.
note: NHS: 999/A&E for these (from search summary of the page).

sentence: The NHS says citalopram should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms.
note: NHS: do not suddenly stop taking it because it may cause withdrawal symptoms.

sentence: A doctor will usually reduce the amount gradually over a few weeks, or longer after a long course.
note: NHS: doctor will gradually reduce dose over a few weeks; longer if taken a long time.

sentence: MedlinePlus lists mood changes, irritability, agitation, dizziness, numbness and tingling or electric-shock sensations as possible withdrawal symptoms.
note: MedlinePlus symptom list.

sentence: The NHS advises avoiding St John's wort, a herbal remedy, because it raises the risk of side effects.
note: NHS: avoid St John's wort.

sentence: It lists aspirin, anticoagulants and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and diclofenac among medicines to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
note: NHS: aspirin, anticoagulants, NSAIDs need checking.

sentence: Sumatriptan, tramadol, medicines that affect heart rhythm and other antidepressants are also on the NHS list to check.
note: NHS: lists these as needing a check.

sentence: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking citalopram, because it can increase the chance of side effects.
note: NHS: best not to drink alcohol as it can increase risk of side effects.

sentence: The NHS says some people with certain heart conditions may not be able to take citalopram.
note: Search summary: main NHS pages describe who should avoid it, including certain heart conditions.

sentence: According to the NHS, citalopram can be used in pregnancy if needed, with the prescriber choosing the lowest amount that works.
note: NHS: can be used during pregnancy if needed; lowest effective dose.

sentence: Taking it late in pregnancy can cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the newborn and may slightly raise the chance of bleeding after delivery.
note: NHS: late-pregnancy exposure; slight bleeding risk after delivery.

sentence: The NHS says this is rare and treatable and is not a reason to stop for most pregnant women.
note: NHS: rare and treatable; not a reason to stop for most women.

sentence: Citalopram can be taken while breastfeeding if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy.
note: NHS: can take while breastfeeding if baby healthy.
